e.t: Abiezer, also rendered Aviezer, is a personal name used for people identified by that name. As a proper name, it does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies a particular person or family connection in the Old Testament Greek translation. This name occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament, in Judges, 2 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. Its exact significance in any individual passage comes from the surrounding verse and context, but the word itself functions as the name Abiezer.

This verb means “catch”: to seize or capture someone or something. It describes an active effort to take hold rather than merely notice or approach. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, appearing once in Job, three times in Proverbs, and once in Hosea. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains taking possession of what is being pursued or trapped.

This adjective means “undissolved” or “indissoluble”—something that has not been separated, broken apart, or undone. It describes a condition of remaining intact rather than expressing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Exodus 36:30. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the exact way this description functions in that sentence must be determined from its context. Its central idea remains something firm, joined, or intact rather than dissolved or separated.

This word is a proper name meaning “Ailam” or “Elam.” It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 66 times across 53 verses, showing that it is used repeatedly as a name. The precise referent in any particular passage depends on the surrounding text, which distinguishes how the name is being used there.

This adjective describes something without order—disorderly rather than arranged or orderly. It points to a condition or manner marked by a lack of proper order. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Proverbs 32:26. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, the word’s exact force in that passage cannot be explained beyond this central meaning. Its basic sense remains clear: it identifies what is disorganized or lacking order.

This adjective describes someone or something that is “unreasoning” or “inconsiderate”—acting without sound judgment or without proper regard for others. It can characterize conduct that lacks thoughtful reflection rather than simply describing a person’s intelligence. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament writings represented here, including Wisdom, 3 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains behavior that is thoughtless, irrational, or heedless of consequences.

This adjective describes something “unspeakable” or “unspeakably many”—something beyond ordinary expression or greatly beyond counting. It can describe either what cannot be adequately put into words or an overwhelming number. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs five times, including three times in Job and twice in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains something extraordinary in expression or amount.

gl: breaking up one’s quarters; marching forth
d: breaking up one’s quarters; marching forth

e.t: This Greek LXX noun refers to breaking up one’s quarters and marching forth. It describes the act of leaving an established camp or position in order to move onward. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and Greek deuterocanonical writings represented here: once in Exodus and twice in 2 Maccabees. Its basic idea is practical movement—dismantling a temporary place of rest or residence and setting out. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “listing of soldiers” or “mustering”—the act of assembling and recording men for military service. It appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 12:43. The word therefore names an organized military gathering or enrollment rather than a person, weapon, or battle itself. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense centers on bringing soldiers together and counting or registering them.

The word means “fly up,” describing movement upward through the air or a rising motion. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Isaiah 16:2. The word’s basic sense is clear, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain precisely what or whom is flying up there. It is a straightforward movement word, centered on upward motion rather than remaining in place or descending.

This Greek LXX verb means “oppose”: to act against someone or something rather than support or follow it. It describes resistance or opposition in a straightforward verbal sense. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic meaning is seen across several kinds of passages rather than being limited to one setting. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on who or what is being opposed.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “soften”: to make something less hard, severe, or rigid. It describes an action or change rather than a person or object, and its ordinary sense can apply wherever something becomes gentler or less harsh. This word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Kings, Job, and Psalms. The exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject.

This Greek LXX verb means “bind” or “patch.” It describes the act of fastening something together or repairing it by covering or joining what is damaged. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament, with one occurrence each in Joshua, Psalms, and Proverbs. Its basic sense is practical and action-oriented: something is secured, mended, or made usable again. The surrounding verse determines whether the action concerns binding an object or patching a damaged part.

This verb means to avert something or turn away from it. It describes an action of directing oneself or something away rather than toward a person, thing, or course. The word appears three times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, each in a different deuterocanonical book. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being turned away and the surrounding sentence.

Apphin, also written Apfin, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 7:12, and is rendered “Apphin” there. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily its identifying function, not a broader concept or idea.

Atergation is a proper name, functioning as the name of a particular person, place, or other named entity rather than as a general word describing an idea or action. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 12:26. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not specify what kind of entity Atergation names. Its exact referent therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “purify”: to make something clean or ritually fit. It describes an action rather than a person or object, and its use belongs to passages about purification in Leviticus and Numbers. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, including passages concerning cleansing and consecration. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the act of purifying.

Achobōr is a personal name, rendered as “Achobōr” or “Akhovor.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs six times across Genesis, 2 Kings, and 1 Chronicles. Because it is a proper name, its ordinary meaning is its role as a personal designation; the surrounding passage is needed to identify which person is being mentioned in a particular occurrence.

Balsan, also rendered Valsan, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Nehemiah 7:7. Because it is a personal name rather than a descriptive word, its basic meaning is the individual designated by that name; the supplied information does not establish an additional meaning or description. The name appears in the LXX and should be kept distinct from similarly rendered names in other biblical language corpora.

This Greek LXX verb means “immerse” or “baptize”: to put someone or something into a surrounding substance. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times—twice in the Old Testament and once in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Gareb, also rendered Gariv, is a proper name used to identify a person. It is not presented here as a common noun describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs three times, in 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, and Jeremiah. The name’s precise identity and significance in any one passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding text.

This noun refers to a sojourner or proselyte—someone living among a people or joining them as an outsider who has come into their community. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, in Exodus and Isaiah. Its basic sense points to a person whose place among the people is defined by residence or religious association rather than original birth among them. The surrounding verse determines which aspect is emphasized in a particular occurrence.

Gergesaios, also rendered Yeryeseos, is a proper name identifying a people or group in the Greek Old Testament. It appears 15 times, across references from Genesis through Nehemiah, as part of the names preserved in the biblical account. The word itself functions as a name rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “womanly,” describing something associated with a woman or feminine qualities. It functions as a descriptive word rather than naming a person by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in Genesis, Deuteronomy, and Esther. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the noun or situation it describes, but its central sense remains connected with what is female, feminine, or characteristic of a woman.

Dareion, also rendered Tharion, is a proper name referring to a person. It is not a descriptive word or action, but a personal designation used in the Greek LXX corpus. This name occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 1:1. Without the surrounding verse text, its particular historical or narrative significance cannot be explained here; the lexical meaning is simply the person’s name. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “mould” or “form”: it describes shaping something into a particular form. As a verb, it focuses on the act of giving an object its shape rather than merely observing the finished result. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both occurrences appearing in Job 33:6. Its normal sense is therefore the intentional forming or fashioning of something. The exact force in Job depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “spread abroad,” describing the act of making something known or causing it to travel widely. It presents spreading as an action rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 37:16. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on something being dispersed or becoming widely known. This LXX word should be understood within its Greek Old Testament setting, rather than treated as a Greek New Testament lexical entry.

This Greek LXX adjective describes someone or something marked by cunning or deceit, especially by misleading others rather than acting openly. It can describe a deceptive character or conduct. The word occurs 25 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, with many occurrences in Psalms and Proverbs. Its repeated use in these books highlights a clear contrast between deceit and the truthful, upright way praised in wisdom and worship. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word introduces a condition: it means “and if” or “unless,” linking what happens to a stated possibility or exception. As a conjunction, it connects clauses so that one statement depends on another. It occurs 1,248 times in the Greek Old Testament represented by the Septuagint, so its exact force is normally understood from the surrounding sentence. Its basic role is conditional rather than naming a person, thing, action, or quality.

This Greek Old Testament verb means to “abandon” or “leave behind.” It describes departing from someone or something so that it is no longer accompanied, supported, or retained. The word can describe people leaving others, or something being forsaken. It appears 171 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, so its basic sense is used broadly across different situations. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on physical departure, desertion, or being left without help.

This word means “twenty,” the number that comes after nineteen and before twenty-one. It is an indeclinable number word, so it functions simply to state a quantity or number. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 253 times, showing regular use in measurements, counts, ages, groups, and other numerical statements. Its meaning remains straightforward wherever it appears; the surrounding words determine what is being counted or measured. The word is found from Genesis through 2 Maccabees in this Greek corpus.

This word is a conjunction expressing an alternative or uncertainty, meaning “whether; or.” It links possible choices, possibilities, or clauses rather than naming a person, thing, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both within Ruth 3:10. Its precise force in a sentence depends on the alternatives being connected, but its normal function is to introduce or join one possibility with another.

This Greek LXX verb means “peep out of”: to look or appear by coming partly out from behind or within something. It describes a brief, limited emergence rather than a full coming into the open. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages in Psalms, Jeremiah, Song of Songs, and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being viewed or emerging there.

This Greek LXX verb means “pillage”: to seize or carry away goods by force, especially in the destruction or defeat of a place. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including Job and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the forceful taking of possessions.

This verb means “terrify”: to cause someone to feel intense fear or alarm. It is an action word describing what one person or force does to another. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented by this LXX corpus, it occurs 13 times, including passages in Leviticus, Job, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Emospheōs is a proper name, referring to a person or group identified by that name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. Its precise referent is tied to the surrounding genealogy or passage, so the name itself does not support a fuller description. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 2:53.

This Greek LXX noun means “ambush”: a concealed position or hidden attack prepared against someone. It refers to a planned military tactic in which people wait out of sight and strike when the opposing group is vulnerable. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, with many occurrences in Joshua’s account of warfare. Its basic sense remains focused on the hidden attack itself, while the surrounding passage determines who prepares it, who is targeted, and how it is carried out.

This Greek LXX noun means “having sworn.” It describes a person who has sworn, pointing to the condition or status expressed by an oath. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Numbers 5:21. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not available, its precise force in that sentence cannot be expanded beyond this basic meaning. In ordinary reading, it identifies someone as having sworn.

This adjective describes something extraordinary or remarkable—something that stands out as unusually impressive or beyond the ordinary. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears five times, all in Job, where it characterizes matters that call attention to the greatness or surprising quality of what is being described. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is clear: remarkable in a way that commands notice.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “use charms; sing to.” It describes an action involving a charm or song directed toward someone or something. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Psalms 57:6 and once in Ecclesiastes 10:11. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic sense is expressed by charming or singing to.

This Greek LXX verb means “head on up,” describing movement toward a higher place or direction. It presents upward travel as an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs five times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in Zechariah, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains directed movement upward.

gl: have a fit; have an epileptic fit
d: have a fit; have an epileptic fit

e.t: This verb means to have a fit, specifically to have an epileptic fit. It describes a physical seizure or fit rather than an action, object, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in 1 Samuel 21:16 and once in Jeremiah 30:19. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the precise role and force of the word in either passage.

Esebon, also rendered Esevon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a named entity appearing 38 times in 38 verses. Its occurrences begin in Numbers and continue through later Old Testament books, including Deuteronomy, Joshua, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Song of Songs. The name itself does not provide a broader ordinary meaning; its specific identity and significance depend on the passage in which it appears.

This adjective describes something that is loud and pleasing to hear. It presents sound as strong enough to be heard clearly while also carrying a quality of pleasantness or beauty. It functions as an adjective describing sound. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Psalm 150:5, so its precise force there belongs to that verse’s surrounding wording. It is rendered “loud” in that occurrence.

e.h: A Personal Name: Eui or Ei
e.t: Eui is a proper name, also rendered Ei. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, in Joshua 13:21 and Ezra 8:15. The name itself gives no further meaning beyond identifying the individual named in each passage; the surrounding verse is needed to know that person’s role in its immediate setting.

This is a Greek LXX proper name, referring to a person named “Ēlkana” or “Ilkana.” It functions as a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs three times, all in 1 Chronicles. The cited references identify its occurrences, but without verse text they do not establish anything more about the person or each passage.

In the Greek Old Testament, this noun means “execution,” referring to the carrying out of a death sentence. It names an act rather than a person or quality, so its meaning focuses on the sentence being carried out. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Samuel 26:16. The reference alone does not provide further context for how the term functions there.

Thekoue, also written Thekue, is a proper name rather than a word describing an idea, action, or quality. It identifies a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament wording, but the available information does not establish which in each passage. This name appears six times in the LXX data, including references in 1 Kings, 2 Kings, Ezra, Jeremiah, and Amos. Its precise identification in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to provoke someone or to become angry. It can describe anger as something stirred up by an offense, or the resulting state of being angry. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 58 times, showing regular use for expressions of anger involving both God and people. Its basic sense remains focused on provocation and anger rather than merely strong emotion in general.

Iachini, also rendered Iakhini, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named person or group rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Numbers 26:12. Its precise reference there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself functions as a name, not as a general vocabulary term.

Ieasi is a proper name used as a specific designation, not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 11:45. The available lexical information gives “Ieasi” as its meaning and does not provide a further descriptive definition. Its precise referent and significance therefore come from the surrounding verse and passage, rather than from a broader lexical sense.

Iemini is a proper name, rendered as “Iemini” in the Greek Old Testament. Unlike a common word that describes an action, quality, or object, this term functions as a specific name rather than a general concept. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in 2 Samuel 16:11 and once in 1 Kings 2:35. The available information identifies the name but does not provide a further meaning or etymological explanation.

This adjective describes someone or something shooting arrows. It points to the action or ability of sending arrows toward a target, rather than naming the arrow itself. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, at Wisdom 16:10. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s exact role in that sentence cannot be stated more specifically, but its central meaning remains connected with shooting arrows.

This word means “equal,” describing something that matches another in measure, standing, condition, or comparison. It can function as an adjective, identifying something as equal, or as an adverb, describing an action done equally or in an equal manner. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 40 times, including passages from Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Job, Ezekiel, Wisdom, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what two things or persons are being compared.

This noun refers to a web or a sail—something made as a sheet or woven surface. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used fourteen times, all within fourteen verses. Its occurrences are concentrated in Exodus, with additional uses in Numbers and Isaiah. The word’s basic meaning remains focused on a physical web or sail, while the exact object intended in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “drop” or “let down,” describing the act of lowering or releasing something. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Judges 6:18. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic idea remains lowering or causing something to descend.

This Greek LXX verb means “shoot down”—to bring someone or something down by shooting. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or general condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Job 30:14, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains direct and forceful downward action caused by shooting.

This verb means “spy on”: to watch or investigate people or a place secretly. It describes deliberate observation carried out to gather information, rather than ordinary seeing. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 14 times, including passages involving people sent to inspect a land or city. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains secret examination for information.

This verb means “mix; mingle.” It describes bringing things together so they are combined rather than remaining separate. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 9:5, so its normal lexical sense is clear even though the available record does not include the verse text or surrounding context. The precise force of the word in that passage must therefore be understood from the sentence and setting in which it appears.

This Greek LXX noun means “hollow,” referring to a hollow or depressed place. It names a physical feature rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs 46 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing across books such as Genesis, Joshua, and Judges. Its precise sense in any particular verse depends on the surrounding description, but its basic idea remains a hollow place or depression. This meaning is distinctively grounded in the LXX usage of this word.

This LXX verb means “whitewash”: to cover a surface with a coating of white material. It describes a practical act of making something appear clean or bright on the outside. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in two passages from Deuteronomy and one from Proverbs. Its basic meaning remains focused on applying whitewash, while the surrounding passage determines the specific object being treated.

Lebna, also rendered Levna, is a proper name rather than a descriptive word with a general everyday meaning. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a named place or person in the book of Joshua; the supplied lexical information establishes the name, while the references show its use there. This name occurs five times across four verses, all in Joshua, from Joshua 10:29 through Joshua 12:15. Its exact referent in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a kneaded mass of dough, especially a cake or baked portion. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Judges 7:13. The word describes a prepared food item rather than an action or quality. Its basic sense is straightforward: something formed by kneading dough, suitable for baking and eating. The precise role of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its translation context.

This Greek LXX adjective means “soft” and can describe the gentle, yielding quality associated with fleece. It points to texture or feel rather than an action or person. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, both times in Proverbs. Its basic sense remains focused on something tender, smooth, or lacking hardness, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being described.

Masbak, also rendered “Mazvak,” is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek text, at 2 Samuel 8:8. Because the name appears only there and the surrounding verse text is not provided here, its specific identity must be understood from that passage’s context.

This word refers to a quilt or bedspread, a covering used on a bed. It is a noun naming the textile itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 8:15. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is a bed covering such as a quilt or spread.

This Greek LXX verb means “put into another dress.” It describes changing someone’s clothing or putting on a different garment, and it functions as an action word. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Amos 5:8. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of changing into another dress or garment.

This verb means to disclose information or inform someone. It describes making something known rather than keeping it hidden. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it appears five times, all in deuterocanonical writings: three times in 2 Maccabees and once each in 3 and 4 Maccabees. Its ordinary sense remains focused on communicating information to another person; the surrounding sentence determines what information is disclosed and to whom.

Nabou, also rendered Navu, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Ezra: once in Ezra 2:29 and once in Ezra 10:43. The available information identifies the name but does not provide the person’s role, background, or significance. Its exact reference in either passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This word refers to a wayfarer—a person traveling along a road or journeying from place to place. It can function as a noun for the traveler himself or as a description of someone who is journeying. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs six times, including passages from Genesis, Judges, Samuel, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its basic sense remains focused on a person identified by travel, while the surrounding verse determines the particular situation being described.

This Greek LXX interjection means “ah me!”—an exclamation expressing distress, grief, or troubled emotion. It is not a statement that names an object or action; instead, it gives voice to a person’s sorrowful reaction. The word occurs 17 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, appearing in passages associated with lament and anguish. Its exact emotional force in any particular verse is clarified by the surrounding words and situation.

This verb means to keep company with someone or converse with them. It describes spending time together through companionship or conversation, rather than merely being near another person. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it can refer generally to social interaction. The word occurs nine times in this LXX corpus, including uses in Proverbs, Daniel, Sirach, and Susanna. Its precise emphasis—companionship or conversation—depends on the surrounding sentence.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Outhi” or “Uthi.” It is not presented as a common description, action, or quality, but as an identifying name. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Ezra 8:14. Because no surrounding verse text is available here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be described further; its lexical meaning is the personal name itself.

This word means “late”. It is an adjective that describes something occurring at a later time, or belonging to a later part of a season or period. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears seven times across seven verses, showing a recurring description of timing rather than an action or person. Its use reaches from Exodus through Zechariah, but the precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding words and passage.

gl: with the whole people; in a mass
d: with the whole people; in a mass

e.t: This Greek LXX adverb means “with the whole people; in a mass.” It describes an action done collectively, involving everyone together rather than individuals separately. The word functions by showing how an action is carried out—together as a whole group. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Deuteronomy 13:17. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding sentence and passage.

The word means “accessible”: it describes something that can be approached, reached, or made available rather than being distant or closed off. As a verb, it expresses the idea of being placed within reach or being available to someone. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs eight times across eight verses, including passages in Sirach and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any sentence depends on what or whom the surrounding passage says is accessible.

This word means “peg,” referring to a physical object. In the Greek Septuagint, it functions as a noun naming that object rather than an action, person, or quality. It appears 23 times in this LXX corpus: twenty occurrences in the Old Testament collection and three in deuterocanonical books. Its ordinary meaning is therefore concrete and stable, though the surrounding verse determines the object’s particular use.

This adjective means “pale,” describing a light or lacking color. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 23:29. Its basic function is to describe appearance or coloration rather than name an action, person, or object by itself. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context, but its ordinary meaning remains a pale or whitened appearance.

This noun refers to a plane-tree, a large leafy tree. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scriptures, it names the tree itself rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs twice in this Greek corpus, once in Genesis and once in Sirach. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its ordinary meaning remains the same: a plane-tree, identified as a distinct kind of tree.

This word means “action,” referring to something a person does or carries out. It is a noun used to speak about deeds or activities rather than a person, place, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 17 times, showing a general term for human activity across several kinds of passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains an action or deed.

This Greek LXX verb means “criticize” or “censure”—to express disapproval of someone or something. As a verb, it describes the act of voicing that disapproval rather than naming the person who receives it. It occurs once in the Greek LXX material represented here, at Sirach 13:22. The precise force in that verse depends on its surrounding wording and passage context.

This verb means to “stand before” others or to be a “ruler over” them. It describes taking a leading or governing position rather than merely being present. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, once in Sirach and once in 1 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on leadership, supervision, or authority, but the central idea is assuming responsibility in front of or over others.

This word means “panel,” referring to a distinct flat section or part of a larger structure. It is a noun, so it names the structural piece itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both within the same verse, 1 Kings 6:34. The word’s basic sense is limited and concrete: a panel or section used as part of something assembled. The surrounding verse supplies the specific object and function, but the word itself identifies the panel as a component.

This adverb means “somehow,” referring to an unspecified way or means by which something happens.
